elements.name: Dynamic Array
elements.what: Contiguous array that grows by amortized capacity doubling (and optionally shrinks), preserving O(1) amortized append and O(1) random access.
elements.problem: Fixed-size arrays force a size guess up front; linked structures sacrifice cache locality and random access. Amortized reallocation gives list flexibility at array speed.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

elements.name: Hash Table
elements.what: Key-value store mapping keys through a hash function into an array of buckets, with collisions resolved by separate chaining or open addressing (linear/quadratic probing, Robin Hood, cuckoo, Swiss-table variants folded here).
elements.problem: Provides expected O(1) lookup, insert, and delete by key when key ordering is not needed, trading memory overhead and worst-case degradation for speed.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

elements.name: B-tree
elements.what: Self-balancing wide-fanout search tree whose nodes hold many keys sized to a block/page, keeping the tree shallow; B+ trees keep all values in linked leaves for range scans.
elements.problem: Binary trees generate one I/O or cache miss per level; matching node size to the storage block minimizes disk/page accesses for ordered indexes, making it the default database and filesystem index.
elements.named_in: Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indexes - Bayer & McCreight (1972)

elements.name: LSM Tree
elements.what: Write-optimized index that batches writes in an in-memory table, flushes them as sorted immutable runs (SSTables), and merges runs in the background via compaction.
elements.problem: In-place index updates (B-trees) turn random writes into random I/O; sequential append plus deferred merge converts write-heavy workloads into sequential I/O at the cost of read amplification.
elements.named_in: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) - O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick, O'Neil (1996)

elements.name: Trie
elements.what: Tree keyed by successive symbols of the key, so all descendants of a node share a common prefix; radix/Patricia variants compress single-child chains into one edge.
elements.problem: Prefix lookup, autocomplete, longest-prefix match (IP routing), and ordered string sets need key-structure-aware indexing that comparison trees and hash tables do not give.
elements.named_in: Trie Memory - Edward Fredkin (1960)

elements.name: Skip List
elements.what: Sorted linked list augmented with probabilistic express lanes at multiple levels, giving expected O(log n) search/insert/delete without rebalancing.
elements.problem: Balanced trees achieve ordered O(log n) operations through intricate rebalancing; randomized levels achieve the same expectation with simpler code and easier concurrent (lock-free) implementation.
elements.named_in: Skip Lists: A Probabilistic Alternative to Balanced Trees - William Pugh (1990)

elements.name: Bloom Filter
elements.what: Bit array plus k hash functions answering approximate set membership with no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate.
elements.problem: Storing full key sets to answer 'definitely absent?' wastes memory; a few bits per element let a component skip expensive lookups (disk reads, cache probes, network calls) for keys that cannot be present.
elements.named_in: Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors - Burton H. Bloom (1970)

elements.name: Count-Min Sketch
elements.what: Sub-linear 2-D counter array indexed by multiple hash functions that answers approximate frequency queries over a stream, with one-sided (over-count) error.
elements.problem: Counting exact per-item frequencies over high-volume streams needs memory proportional to distinct items; a fixed small sketch bounds error probabilistically for heavy-hitter and frequency estimation.
elements.named_in: An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications - Cormode & Muthukrishnan (2005)

elements.name: HyperLogLog
elements.what: Cardinality-estimation sketch that hashes items and records maximum leading-zero runs in a small register array, estimating distinct counts within a few percent using kilobytes.
elements.problem: Exact distinct-count over large streams requires storing every seen key; probabilistic register merging gives mergeable, fixed-memory cardinality estimates (unique visitors, distinct keys).
elements.named_in: HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm - Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet, Meunier (2007)

elements.name: Bitmap / Bitset
elements.what: Dense array of bits representing set membership or boolean flags by index, supporting bulk bitwise set operations word-at-a-time; compressed variants (Roaring, WAH) handle sparse ranges.
elements.problem: Sets over a bounded integer universe cost far less as one bit per element than as pointer structures, and AND/OR/NOT over machine words gives vectorized set algebra (allocator maps, DB bitmap indexes, ECS masks).
elements.named_in: Programming Pearls - Jon Bentley (1986)

elements.name: Disjoint-Set (Union-Find)
elements.what: Forest of trees tracking a partition of elements into disjoint sets, with union-by-rank and path compression making find/union near-constant amortized.
elements.problem: Incremental equivalence tracking (connected components, type unification, Kruskal's MST, image segmentation) needs merge-and-query on partitions far faster than recomputing reachability.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

elements.name: Binary Heap (Priority Queue)
elements.what: Implicit complete binary tree stored in an array maintaining the heap order property, giving O(log n) insert and extract-min/max with no pointers.
elements.problem: Schedulers, event queues, Dijkstra-style algorithms, and timer systems repeatedly need the next-highest-priority item without keeping the whole collection sorted.
elements.named_in: Algorithm 232: Heapsort - J. W. J. Williams (1964)

elements.name: Deque
elements.what: Sequence container supporting O(1) insertion and removal at both ends, typically as a ring buffer or blocked array.
elements.problem: Sliding windows, work-stealing schedulers, and undo histories need queue and stack behavior simultaneously; neither a plain stack nor a FIFO queue suffices.
elements.named_in: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1: Fundamental Algorithms - Donald Knuth (1968)

elements.name: Intrusive Linked List
elements.what: Linked list whose link fields live inside the stored objects themselves rather than in externally allocated nodes, so linking requires no allocation.
elements.problem: Kernel, embedded, and real-time code cannot afford per-node heap allocation or double indirection; embedding links gives allocation-free O(1) insert/remove and lets one object sit on several lists.
elements.named_in: Boost.Intrusive library documentation - Ion Gaztanaga, Olaf Krzikalla

elements.name: Free List
elements.what: Linked list threaded through unused memory blocks or object slots themselves, from which an allocator pops on allocate and onto which it pushes on free.
elements.problem: Recycling fixed-size blocks in O(1) without heap traffic or fragmentation bookkeeping; the backbone of pool allocators, slab allocators, and embedded memory managers.
elements.named_in: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1: Fundamental Algorithms - Donald Knuth (1968)

elements.name: Rope
elements.what: Balanced binary tree of string fragments representing a long string, making concatenation, insertion, and splitting O(log n) instead of O(n) copies.
elements.problem: Flat strings make every edit of a large text a full copy; editors and string-heavy systems need sublinear splice operations and cheap substring sharing.
elements.named_in: Ropes: an Alternative to Strings - Boehm, Atkinson, Plass (1995)

elements.name: Gap Buffer
elements.what: Contiguous text buffer with a movable gap of free space at the cursor position, making localized insertions and deletions O(1) until the gap moves or fills.
elements.problem: Text editing clusters around a cursor; keeping the free space there converts the common-case edit from an O(n) array shift into an in-place write (Emacs's buffer representation).
elements.named_in: The Craft of Text Editing - Craig A. Finseth (1991)

elements.name: Piece Table
elements.what: Edit representation keeping the original file and an append-only add buffer immutable, with the document described as a sequence of pieces (spans) into the two buffers.
elements.problem: Editors need fast arbitrary edits, cheap undo, and untouched original file data; recording edits as span descriptors avoids moving text and makes undo a piece-list operation.
elements.named_in: Data Structures for Text Sequences - Charles Crowley (1998)

elements.name: Merkle Tree
elements.what: Tree whose leaves are hashes of data blocks and whose internal nodes hash their children, so one root hash authenticates the whole set and any block is verifiable with a log-length path.
elements.problem: Verifying integrity or divergence of large or distributed data sets without transferring them; enables efficient tamper-evidence, sync anti-entropy, and inclusion proofs (Git, ZFS, certificate transparency, blockchains).
elements.named_in: A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function - Ralph Merkle (1987)

elements.name: Consistent Hashing
elements.what: Hashing scheme placing keys and buckets on the same ring so each key maps to the nearest bucket, remapping only ~1/n of keys when a bucket joins or leaves; virtual nodes smooth the load.
elements.problem: Modulo hashing reshuffles nearly every key when the bucket count changes; caches and partitioned stores need key-to-node assignment that is stable under membership churn.
elements.named_in: Consistent Hashing and Random Trees: Distributed Caching Protocols for Relieving Hot Spots on the World Wide Web - Karger et al. (1997)
elements.borderline: The ring structure is implementable inside one component (IN); its use as a cluster-partitioning scheme shades architectural - parked companion entry for Phase 3.

elements.name: Inverted Index
elements.what: Mapping from each term to the sorted list of documents (and positions) containing it, the core structure of full-text search engines.
elements.problem: Scanning documents per query is linear in corpus size; inverting the term-document relation makes multi-term queries an intersection/union of postings lists.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Information Retrieval - Manning, Raghavan, Schutze (2008)

elements.name: LRU Cache
elements.what: Bounded map coupling a hash table with a recency-ordered doubly linked list so lookup, insert, and evict-least-recently-used are all O(1).
elements.problem: Fixed-size caches must pick a victim on overflow; recency ordering approximates future usefulness cheaply, and the hash-plus-list composition makes the policy constant-time.
elements.named_in: Evaluation Techniques for Storage Hierarchies - Mattson, Gecsei, Slutz, Traiger (1970)

elements.name: Ring Buffer
elements.what: Fixed-size array with wrapping head and tail indices forming a FIFO that never moves data or allocates, naturally overwriting or blocking when full.
elements.problem: Producer-consumer handoff (ISR-to-task, audio, logging, SPSC queues) needs constant-time bounded buffering without allocation; wrap-around indexing gives it with two indices.
elements.named_in: Making Embedded Systems: Design Patterns for Great Software - Elecia White (2024)
elements.borderline: Shared with the data-flow scout by charter design; included here as the structural entry.

elements.name: Quadtree / Octree
elements.what: Hierarchical spatial partition recursively subdividing 2D space into four quadrants (or 3D into eight octants) until cells meet an occupancy or depth bound.
elements.problem: Spatial queries (culling, collision broad-phase, image regions, point clouds) over non-uniform data need adaptive subdivision that concentrates resolution where objects cluster.
elements.named_in: Quad Trees: A Data Structure for Retrieval on Composite Keys - Finkel & Bentley (1974)

elements.name: k-d Tree
elements.what: Binary space-partitioning tree that splits points on alternating coordinate axes, supporting nearest-neighbor and orthogonal range queries in low dimensions.
elements.problem: Nearest-neighbor and range search over point sets is linear without an index; axis-aligned recursive splits prune most of the space per query.
elements.named_in: Multidimensional Binary Search Trees Used for Associative Searching - Jon Bentley (1975)

elements.name: Bounding Volume Hierarchy
elements.what: Tree whose nodes are bounding volumes (typically AABBs) enclosing their children, with scene objects at the leaves, letting intersection queries prune whole subtrees.
elements.problem: Ray tracing and collision detection against thousands of objects cannot test each primitive; hierarchical bounds reduce intersection tests to a logarithmic descent.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Rendering - Akenine-Moller, Haines, Hoffman (2018)

elements.name: Uniform Spatial Hash Grid
elements.what: Partition of space into uniform cells whose coordinates hash into buckets of contained objects, so neighborhood queries examine only nearby cells.
elements.problem: Broad-phase collision and proximity queries need O(1) neighbor lookup for roughly uniformly-sized objects without the build cost or pointer-chasing of trees.
elements.named_in: Optimized Spatial Hashing for Collision Detection of Deformable Objects - Teschner et al. (2003)

elements.name: R-tree
elements.what: Balanced B-tree-like index of minimum bounding rectangles that may overlap, grouping nearby spatial objects for disk-friendly window and containment queries.
elements.problem: Databases need paged, balanced indexing of extended spatial objects (rectangles, polygons) where point-based partitions fail; the standard spatial index of GIS databases.
elements.named_in: R-Trees: A Dynamic Index Structure for Spatial Searching - Antonin Guttman (1984)

elements.name: Interval Tree
elements.what: Search tree over intervals (typically a BST augmented with subtree max-endpoints) answering which stored intervals overlap a query point or interval in O(log n + k).
elements.problem: Schedulers, editors (marker ranges), genomics, and calendars repeatedly ask 'what overlaps this range?', which sorted lists answer only by linear scan.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
elements.borderline: Charter-flagged: kept IN - a recurring designer-reachable role (overlap queries), not just an algorithmics exercise.

elements.name: Segment Tree
elements.what: Complete binary tree over an array where each node stores an aggregate (sum, min, max) of its range, giving O(log n) range queries and point/range updates.
elements.problem: Alternating range-aggregate queries and updates over an array defeat both prefix-sum arrays (slow update) and raw arrays (slow query); the tree balances the two.
elements.named_in: Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications - de Berg, Cheong, van Kreveld, Overmars (2008)
elements.borderline: Charter-flagged research-zoo borderline: kept IN - named, recurring, and reached-for by role (range aggregate index) well beyond competitive programming; variants folded.

elements.name: Fenwick Tree
elements.what: Implicit array-based tree exploiting binary index decomposition to maintain prefix sums with O(log n) point update and prefix query in n words of memory.
elements.problem: The prefix-sum-with-updates role of a segment tree, in a fraction of the memory and code, when only invertible aggregates (sums, counts) are needed.
elements.named_in: A New Data Structure for Cumulative Frequency Tables - Peter Fenwick (1994)
elements.borderline: Near the research-zoo line; included because it is the named lighter-weight alternative designers actually reach for over segment trees for cumulative counts.

elements.name: Adjacency List / Adjacency Matrix
elements.what: The two canonical in-memory graph representations: per-vertex edge lists (sparse-friendly, Theta(V+E) space) versus a V-by-V boolean/weight matrix (dense-friendly, O(1) edge test).
elements.problem: Every graph-processing component must commit to an edge-storage layout; the list/matrix choice trades memory and iteration locality against constant-time adjacency tests.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
elements.borderline: Charter-flagged: a representation choice rather than a single structure; kept as ONE element covering the named pair since the choice itself is the recurring design act.

elements.name: Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT)
aka: G-Counter / PN-Counter / G-Set / OR-Set / LWW-Register / RGA (family members, folded)
elements.what: Family of replicated data types (counters, sets, registers, sequences) whose merge operations are commutative/associative/idempotent, so concurrently edited replicas converge without coordination.
elements.problem: Multi-writer replication without locks or consensus produces conflicts; algebraically merge-safe state lets offline-first apps and collaborative editors converge deterministically.
elements.named_in: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types - Shapiro, Preguica, Baquero, Zawirski (2011)
elements.borderline: Charter mandates ONE element for the family; each replica's type is implementable in one component (IN), though the replication context shades distributed-systems territory.

elements.name: Linked List
elements.what: Sequence of nodes each holding an element and a pointer to the next (and optionally previous) node, giving O(1) insertion/removal at a known position without element movement.
elements.problem: Sequences with frequent mid-stream splicing, stable element addresses, or no contiguous memory (allocators, kernels) cannot use arrays; pointer links trade locality for splice freedom.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
elements.borderline: Near the lower altitude floor (elementary ADT) but unambiguously named, recurring, and a deliberate design choice versus arrays; kept IN.

elements.name: Stack
elements.what: Last-in-first-out collection with push/pop/peek at one end, whether array- or list-backed.
elements.problem: Nested and reversible processes - call frames, undo, parsing, DFS, expression evaluation - need most-recent-first access as a structural guarantee.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
elements.borderline: Elementary ADT at the band's floor; kept IN because designers reach for 'a stack' by role constantly and it anchors many other elements.

elements.name: Queue (FIFO)
elements.what: First-in-first-out collection with enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head, array- or list-backed.
elements.problem: Order-preserving buffering between producers and consumers - task queues, BFS frontiers, request pipelines - requires arrival-order service as a structural guarantee.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
elements.borderline: Elementary ADT at the band's floor; kept IN as the in-process structure (the message-queue mechanism and broker topology belong to other scouts/Phase 3).

elements.name: Binary Search Tree
aka: treap / splay tree (research variants, sibling corpus)
elements.what: Binary tree maintaining the search-order invariant (left < node < right); self-balancing variants (red-black, AVL) guarantee O(log n) ordered operations.
elements.problem: Ordered maps/sets needing sorted iteration, predecessor/successor, and range queries - which hash tables cannot provide - with logarithmic worst-case bounds (std::map, kernel schedulers).
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

elements.name: Suffix Array
elements.what: Sorted array of all suffix start positions of a text, supporting binary-search substring queries; the array-based, cache-friendly successor to the suffix tree.
elements.problem: Repeated arbitrary-substring search over a fixed large text (bioinformatics, plagiarism detection, search indexing) needs a full-text index cheaper than a suffix tree's pointers.
elements.named_in: Suffix Arrays: A New Method for On-Line String Searches - Manber & Myers (1990)
elements.borderline: Shades research-zoo; kept IN as the designer-reachable full-text-substring-index role, with suffix tree and FM-index folded as variants.

elements.name: Hash Array Mapped Trie (HAMT)
elements.what: Trie over hash-code bit chunks using per-node bitmaps to compress sparse children, giving an efficiently persistent (structurally shared, immutable) hash map.
elements.problem: Immutable/functional programs need maps whose 'updates' return new versions in O(log n) time and memory via structural sharing rather than full copies (Clojure, Scala, Immutable.js collections).
elements.named_in: Ideal Hash Trees - Phil Bagwell (2001)

elements.name: t-digest
elements.what: Mergeable sketch of a numeric distribution built from size-varying centroid clusters, estimating quantiles (esp. extreme percentiles) accurately in constant memory.
elements.problem: Monitoring systems need p99/p999 latency over unbounded streams and across shards; exact quantiles require storing all samples, and fixed-bin histograms lose tail accuracy.
elements.named_in: Computing Extremely Accurate Quantiles Using t-Digests - Dunning & Ertl (2019)

elements.name: MinHash
elements.what: Similarity sketch storing the minimum hash values of a set under many hash functions, so sketch agreement estimates Jaccard similarity between sets.
elements.problem: Near-duplicate detection and similarity search over huge document/set collections cannot compare full sets pairwise; small fixed sketches make similarity estimable in constant time.
elements.named_in: On the Resemblance and Containment of Documents - Andrei Broder (1997)

elements.name: Sparse Set
elements.what: Pair of arrays (dense packed elements plus sparse index-by-value) representing an integer set with O(1) insert, delete, membership, and clear, and cache-friendly iteration over only the members.
elements.problem: Sets over a bounded integer universe that are cleared and iterated constantly (compiler live-sets, ECS component membership) need O(1) clear and dense iteration, which bitmaps and hash sets lack.
elements.named_in: An Efficient Representation for Sparse Sets - Briggs & Torczon (1993)

elements.name: Slot Map
elements.what: Contiguous object pool addressed by stable keys that pair a slot index with a generation counter, so freed-and-reused slots invalidate stale handles while keeping O(1) access and dense iteration.
elements.problem: Game and systems code needs stable, dangle-proof references into pools of frequently created/destroyed objects without pointer invalidation or use-after-free; generations make stale handles detectable.
elements.named_in: slot_map Container in C++ (WG21 P0661) - Allan Deutsch (2017)

parked_architecture.name: Distributed hash table (Chord/Kademlia/DHT)
parked_architecture.why: System-level overlay topology built atop consistent hashing; the routing overlay is a multi-node structure, not implementable inside one component.

parked_architecture.name: Sharding / data partitioning scheme
parked_architecture.why: System-level data-distribution decision across nodes; the in-process hash-ring structure is cataloged, the cluster partitioning strategy is Phase 3's.

parked_architecture.name: Distributed replicated log (Kafka-style commit log)
parked_architecture.why: As a cluster-wide ordering/replication backbone it is a topology; the in-process append-only log / WAL mechanism belongs to the persistence scout.

parked_architecture.name: Blockchain / Merkle-chained distributed ledger
parked_architecture.why: System-of-nodes construct composing Merkle trees with consensus; the Merkle tree itself is cataloged as the design element.

parked_architecture.name: Search-engine index tier (index + query fan-out architecture)
parked_architecture.why: The inverted index is cataloged; the sharded index-serving tier around it is architecture.

excluded_notable.name: B+ tree, counting/cuckoo/XOR filters, Roaring bitmap, red-black/AVL/splay/treap, Patricia/radix trie, Fibonacci/pairing heaps, suffix tree, octree, R* variants, CHAMP, HLL++
excluded_notable.why: Variant-zoo entries folded into their role-level elements' aka/notes per charter; the datastructures sibling corpus owns variant-level enumeration.

excluded_notable.name: Lock-free queue (Michael-Scott), concurrent hash map, RCU-protected structures
excluded_notable.why: Real designer-reachable structures but concurrency-mechanism-first; left to the execution-concurrency scout to avoid duplicate ids (flagged as a cross-scout dependency, not dropped).

excluded_notable.name: Write-ahead log / append-only log
excluded_notable.why: Persistence-durability mechanism, not a container role; assumed owned by the persistence scout (verify coverage at merge).

excluded_notable.name: Timer wheel
excluded_notable.why: Scheduling-and-time element (Varghese & Lauck 1987); scheduling scout territory - verify coverage at merge.

excluded_notable.name: Z-order curve / Morton code, geohash
excluded_notable.why: Spatial key-encoding techniques rather than container structures; borderline algorithmic - recorded for a possible follow-up sweep.

excluded_notable.name: Wavelet tree, van Emde Boas tree, Judy array, finger tree, succinct/compressed structures (FM-index et al.)
excluded_notable.why: Research-zoo granularity; not designer-role vocabulary outside specialist niches - sibling corpus territory.

excluded_notable.name: Sorting/search algorithm families (quicksort, timsort, binary search)
excluded_notable.why: Algorithms, not structures; charter covers structures a designer reaches for by role.

notes: Coverage: all 31 charter-listed items delivered (quadtree/octree merged as one entry per charter phrasing; adjacency list/matrix as ONE representation-choice element; CRDT family as ONE). Additions beyond the explicit list, all inside the charter's 'designer reaches for by role' frame: linked list, stack, queue, binary search tree (floor-of-band ADTs, borderline-tagged), Fenwick tree, suffix array, R-tree, HAMT, t-digest, MinHash, sparse set, slot map. DECISIONS LOGGED: (1) trie fold - radix/Patricia/prefix-tree folded into one trie element (same mechanism, compression variants); (2) segment tree - kept IN despite research-zoo flag, borderline-tagged (recurring range-aggregate role); Fenwick kept separately since it is the named lighter alternative designers choose BETWEEN, not a variant of the same node structure; (3) interval tree kept IN, borderline-tagged; (4) quadtree/octree one element (dimension analogues of one mechanism); (5) stack/queue/linked-list/BST included at the band floor with honest borderline tags per over-inclusion rule; (6) ring buffer included despite data-flow scout overlap per charter, kind=data-flow-buffering, named_in corpus work 'white'; (7) lock-free structures, WAL, and timer wheel deliberately deferred to sibling scouts - MERGE COORDINATOR MUST VERIFY those scouts covered them. named_in_corpus_id is null everywhere except ring-buffer ('white'): CLRS/TAOCP/Sedgewick/original DS papers are not corpus works (grep of work_ids.tsv confirmed). Confidence: 42 established from deep familiarity of canonical sources, 1 spot-checked live (slot map: WG21 P0661 + C++Now 2017 confirmed via web search this session).
